claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison to prior microarray data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The study added three clusters of epithelial cells from the vas deferens, which appear to be analogous to epididymal principal cells based on shared markers.
claims.source: To this initial set of six epididymal clusters, we added three clusters of epithelial cells from the vas deferens (Figure 3A), which appear in our dataset (based on shared markers) to be analogous to epididymal principal cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis and marker gene expression.

claims.claim: The second round of clustering of principal cells was dominated by the anatomical origin of principal cells, separating cells from the caput, corpus, cauda, and vas deferens.
claims.source: The second round of clustering was again dominated by the anatomical origin of principal cells, separating cells from the caput, corpus, cauda, and vas deferens (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: At higher resolution, cells from each anatomic region could be further subdivided into three to four subtypes.
claims.source: Moreover, at this resolution, cells from each anatomic region could be further subdivided into three to four subtypes (Figure 3B), largely reflecting further subspecialization of cells in the various compartmentalized epididymal segments (Johnston et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Cells corresponding to the mouse initial segment were readily identified as a subset of principal cells from the caput dissection based on their expression of genes previously associated with segment 1.
claims.source: For instance, cells corresponding to the mouse initial segment were readily identified as a subset of principal cells from the caput dissection based on their expression of genes (RNase10, Cst11, Lcn2, Mfge8, and others) previously associated with segment 1 (Johnston et al., 2005), and were distinguished from other cells from more distal segments of the caput epididymis (Lcn2 and Defb15 for segments 3–4, etc.).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis and comparison to prior microarray data.

claims.claim: The subclustering of principal cells is concordant with prior functional and molecular studies of epididymal segmentation.
claims.source: Overall, our subclustering is concordant with prior functional and molecular studies of epididymal segmentation, and supports the notion that the anatomical segmentation of the epididymis generates multiple distinct microenvironments that sperm experience during post-testicular maturation (Domeniconi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparison to prior studies and the subclustering analysis.

claims.claim: The anatomical segmentation of the epididymis generates multiple distinct microenvironments that sperm experience during post-testicular maturation.
claims.source: Overall, our subclustering is concordant with prior functional and molecular studies of epididymal segmentation, and supports the notion that the anatomical segmentation of the epididymis generates multiple distinct microenvironments that sperm experience during post-testicular maturation (Domeniconi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The genes that define principal cells from any given segment tend to be members of multi-gene families encoded in genomic clusters of many paralogous genes.
claims.source: As is clear from many prior studies of epididymal gene regulation (Guyonnet et al., 2009; Hales et al., 1980; Hall et al., 2007; Jelinsky et al., 2007; Jervis and Robaire, 2001; Johnston et al., 2005; Papp et al., 1995; Ribeiro et al., 2016; Thimon et al., 2007), the genes that define principal cells from any given segment tend to be members of multi-gene families encoded in genomic clusters of many paralogous genes (Figure 3D–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: These gene clusters include gene families encoding serine protease inhibitors, antimicrobial defensin peptides, cysteine-rich peptides involved in glycocalyx maturation, small molecule-binding lipocalins, aldo-keto reductases, and RNaseA family members.
claims.source: These clusters include gene families encoding serine protease inhibitors, antimicrobial defensin peptides, cysteine-rich peptides involved in glycocalyx maturation, small molecule-binding lipocalins, aldo-keto reductases, and RNaseA family members.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The encoded proteins play roles throughout the male reproductive tract, both locally in the epididymal lumen as well as in downstream regions of the male reproductive tract, or even in the female reproductive tract.
claims.source: The encoded proteins play roles throughout the male reproductive tract, both locally in the epididymal lumen as well as in downstream regions of the male reproductive tract, or even in the female reproductive tract (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in reproductive biology.

claims.claim: A number of region-specific proteins, including various metabolic enzymes, small-molecule-binding proteins, and defensins, end up decorating the sperm surface.
claims.source: Curiously, a number of these region-specific proteins, including various metabolic enzymes, small-molecule-binding proteins, and defensins, also end up decorating the sperm surface.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in reproductive biology.

claims.claim: Few of the marker genes for the vas deferens are encoded in large multi-gene families, with two major exceptions being members of gene families encoding serine protease inhibitors and crystallin proteins.
claims.source: In contrast to the principal cells of the epididymis, few of the marker genes for the vas deferens are encoded in large multi-gene families, with two major exceptions being members of gene families encoding serine protease inhibitors (Akr1b7, Akr1c1) (Jagoe et al., 2013) and crystallin proteins (Crygb, Crygc).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data for vas deferens principal cells.

claims.claim: Genes enriched in the vas deferens included various transmembrane transporters and signaling molecules.
claims.source: Instead, genes enriched in the vas deferens included various transmembrane transporters (Abcg2, Fxyd4, Aqp2, etc.) and signaling molecules (Plac8, Ptgr1, Ptges, Ptgs2, Prlr, Cited1, Pcbd1, Comt, Slco2a1, etc.).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data for vas deferens principal cells.

claims.claim: Vas deferens clusters were enriched for expression of nuclear-encoded genes involved in mitochondrial energy production.
claims.source: Vas deferens clusters were also enriched for expression of nuclear-encoded genes involved in mitochondrial energy production (Atp5g1, Uqcr10, Ndufa3, Cox6b1, Ndufa7, Ndufa11, Atp5e, Mrpl33, etc.), but this was not unique to the vas deferens – across the epididymis, mitochondrial energy production was enriched in principal, clear, and muscle cells, and depleted in basal, immune, endothelial, and stromal cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Across the epididymis, mitochondrial energy production was enriched in principal, clear, and muscle cells, and depleted in basal, immune, endothelial, and stromal cells.
claims.source: Vas deferens clusters were also enriched for expression of nuclear-encoded genes involved in mitochondrial energy production (Atp5g1, Uqcr10, Ndufa3, Cox6b1, Ndufa7, Ndufa11, Atp5e, Mrpl33, etc.), but this was not unique to the vas deferens – across the epididymis, mitochondrial energy production was enriched in principal, clear, and muscle cells, and depleted in basal, immune, endothelial, and stromal cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Abcg2 is a notable marker of vas deferens epithelial cells.
claims.source: We were particularly interested in one notable marker of vas deferens epithelial cells, Abcg2, which encodes a xenobiotic transporter whose functions are best-understood in the placenta.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data for vas deferens principal cells.

claims.claim: Abcg2 encodes a xenobiotic transporter whose functions are best-understood in the placenta.
claims.source: We were particularly interested in one notable marker of vas deferens epithelial cells, Abcg2, which encodes a xenobiotic transporter whose functions are best-understood in the placenta.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the Abcg2 protein.

claims.claim: Abcg2 is localized to the apical end of syncitiotrophoblast cells of the human placenta, where it protects the developing fetus by pumping small molecules back into the maternal circulation.
claims.source: Abcg2 is localized to the apical end of syncitiotrophoblast cells of the human placenta, where it protects the developing fetus by pumping small molecules back into the maternal circulation, thereby preventing xenobiotics from crossing the placental barrier (Wang et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Abcg2 has been implicated in sperm function, as it is localized on the sperm surface where it is proposed to play a role in modulating the levels/localization of specific membrane lipids.
claims.source: Abcg2 has also been implicated in sperm function, as it is localized on the sperm surface where it is proposed to play a role in modulating the levels/localization of specific membrane lipids (Caballero et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: ABC-class transporters such as Abcg2 are typically localized to the apical end of polarized epithelia.
claims.source: Although the function of Abcg2 in the vas deferens is unclear, we note that ABC-class transporters such as Abcg2 are typically localized to the apical end of polarized epithelia, which we confirmed with immunofluorescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC-class transporters, confirmed by immunofluorescence in this study.

claims.claim: Abcg2 expression in the vas deferens would be predicted to pump small molecules into the lumen, rather than clearing them out.
claims.source: This suggests that Abcg2 expression in the vas deferens would be predicted to pump small molecules into the lumen, rather than clearing them out.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known localization of ABC-class transporters and the immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: The data suggest an unappreciated role for Abcg2 in concentrating some factor(s) in the lumen of the vas deferens.
claims.source: As ABC class transporters such as Abcg2 are known to pump some endogenously synthesized molecules (such as heme), our data suggest an unappreciated role for this protein in concentrating some factor(s) in the lumen of the vas deferens.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the expression and localization of Abcg2 in the vas deferens.

claims.claim: Clear cells are largely responsible for providing an acidic luminal environment that ensures that sperm remain quiescent until mating occurs.
claims.source: Clear cells are largely responsible for one of the best-known functions of the epididymis, which is to provide an acidic luminal environment that ensures that sperm remain quiescent until mating occurs (Breton et al., 1998; Breton et al., 1999; Brown et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in reproductive biology, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Clear cells accomplish luminal acidification via high-level expression of vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) genes.
claims.source: This function is accomplished via high-level expression of vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) genes (Breton and Brown, 2013; Breton et al., 1996; Carr and Acott, 1984; Hermo et al., 2000), and clear cells are readily identified in our dataset by expression of the V-ATPase-encoding marker genes Atp6v0c, Atpv1e1, and Atp6v1a (Figure 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in reproductive biology, supported by citations and confirmed by the single-cell RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Clear cells are readily identified in the dataset by expression of the V-ATPase-encoding marker genes Atp6v0c, Atpv1e1, and Atp6v1a.
claims.source: This function is accomplished via high-level expression of vacuolar ATPase (V-ATPase) genes (Breton and Brown, 2013; Breton et al., 1996; Carr and Acott, 1984; Hermo et al., 2000), and clear cells are readily identified in our dataset by expression of the V-ATPase-encoding marker genes Atp6v0c, Atpv1e1, and Atp6v1a (Figure 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claims.claim: Clear cells were enriched for genes involved in energy metabolism and membrane trafficking.
claims.source: In addition to expressing genes encoding V-ATPase subunits and V-ATPase-interacting proteins (Dmxl1), clear cells were enriched for genes involved in a wide range of functions, with the two most prominent being energy metabolism and membrane trafficking.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data for clear cells.

claims.claim: Clear cells express high levels of genes involved in metabolic energy production, presumably to provide the high levels of ATP needed to power the acidification of the epididymal lumen.
claims.source: In the former case, similar to vas deferens principal cells, clear cells also express high levels of genes involved in metabolic energy production, presumably serving to provide the high levels of ATP needed to power the acidification of the epididymal lumen.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data and represents a logical inference about the function of these genes.

claims.claim: Clear cells are characterized by high expression of various membrane trafficking genes, consistent with the important role for active membrane recycling/endocytosis in localization of the vacuolar ATPase to clear cell microvilli.
claims.source: In addition to this elevated energy production, clear cells are also characterized by high expression of various membrane trafficking genes (Dab2, Ap1s3, Arf3, Stx7, Cdc42se2). This is consistent with the important role for active membrane recycling/endocytosis in localization of the vacuolar ATPase to clear cell microvilli (Breton and Brown, 2013; Shum et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Reclustering of clear cells revealed three clear cell subclusters.
claims.source: To explore diversity among epididymal clear cells, we isolated and reclustered them (Figure 4A) as described above for principal cells, finding three clear cell subclusters (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Two clear cell subclusters included clear cells from throughout the epididymis, while Cluster 2 was comprised entirely of clear cells from the caput and corpus epididymis.
claims.source: Two of these clusters included clear cells from throughout the epididymis, while Cluster 2 was comprised entirely of clear cells from the caput and corpus epididymis (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Clear cell Cluster 2 was distinguished by the expression of Iapp, encoding islet amyloid polypeptide, or Amylin.
claims.source: This subcluster was distinguished by the expression of a small number of genes, with one standout marker gene: Iapp, encoding islet amyloid polypeptide, or Amylin (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Amylin labels a subset of V-ATPase-positive clear cells in the caput and the corpus epididymis, and these cells were undetectable in the cauda or vas deferens.
claims.source: To validate these potentially distinct clear cell types, we stained epididymal tissue sections for a general clear cell marker (V-ATPase) and for Amylin. Consistent with the single-cell expression profiles, we find that Amylin labels a subset of V-ATPase-positive clear cells in the caput and the corpus epididymis, and that these cells were undetectable in the cauda or vas deferens (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: It seems unlikely that Amylin-positive clear cells correspond to the classical clear cell subtypes known as 'narrow' and 'apical' cells, which are uniquely found in the initial segment of the caput epididymis.
claims.source: We note that it seems unlikely that Amylin-positive clear cells correspond to the classical clear cell subtypes known as 'narrow' and 'apical' cells, which are uniquely found in the initial segment of the caput epididymis (Abou-Haïla and Fain-Maurel, 1984; Adamali and Hermo, 1996; Breton et al., 2016; Sun and Flickinger, 1979; Sun and Flickinger, 1980), as we find Amylin-positive cells outside of the initial segment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the immunofluorescence data showing Amylin-positive cells outside the initial segment.

claims.claim: Only a subset of clear cells in any given cross-section were Amylin-positive.
claims.source: Together with the observation that only a subset of clear cells in any given cross-section were Amylin-positive, our data suggest the intriguing possibility that Amylin-positive cells represent a functionally distinct subclass of clear cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The data suggest the intriguing possibility that Amylin-positive cells represent a functionally distinct subclass of clear cells.
claims.source: Together with the observation that only a subset of clear cells in any given cross-section were Amylin-positive, our data suggest the intriguing possibility that Amylin-positive cells represent a functionally distinct subclass of clear cells.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the single-cell RNA-seq and immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: Basal cells are so-named for the fact that their cell bodies are primarily localized on the basal surface of the tube.
claims.source: The third major cell type consists of the basal cells, so-named for the fact that their cell bodies are primarily localized on the basal surface of the tube, although their cytoplasmic processes have been shown to reach the lumen in some regions of the epididymis (Shum et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in reproductive biology, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Basal cell cytoplasmic processes have been shown to reach the lumen in some regions of the epididymis.
claims.source: The third major cell type consists of the basal cells, so-named for the fact that their cell bodies are primarily localized on the basal surface of the tube, although their cytoplasmic processes have been shown to reach the lumen in some regions of the epididymis (Shum et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Basal cells are believed to play an important role in maintaining the structural integrity of the blood-epididymis barrier.
claims.source: Basal cells are believed to play an important role in maintaining the structural integrity of the blood-epididymis barrier, and it has been proposed that they may be adult stem cells for the epididymal epithelium (Mandon et al., 2015; Pinel et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: It has been proposed that basal cells may be adult stem cells for the epididymal epithelium.
claims.source: Basal cells are believed to play an important role in maintaining the structural integrity of the blood-epididymis barrier, and it has been proposed that they may be adult stem cells for the epididymal epithelium (Mandon et al., 2015; Pinel et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and represents a hypothesis in the field.

claims.claim: Three clusters of basal cells were identified in the dataset based on the shared expression of marker genes including Itga6 and Krt14.
claims.source: Three clusters of basal cells were identified in our dataset based on the shared expression of marker genes including Itga6 and Krt14 (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2C–D.

claims.claim: Basal cells co-expressed a wide variety of genes involved in cell adhesion and intercellular signaling.
claims.source: Co-expressed with these genes were a wide variety of genes involved in cell adhesion (Bcam, Gja1, Cldn1, Cldn4, Epcam, Sfn, Cdh16, Itgb6) and intercellular signaling (Adm, Egfr, Hbegf, Nrg1, Ctgf, Dll1, Egfl6, Cd44, Cd9, Tacstd2), consistent with a recent genome-wide analysis of isolated rat basal cells (Mandon et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Basal cells exhibited high level expression of several genes involved in membrane trafficking and lipid metabolism, suggesting that basal cells may exhibit more dynamic membrane remodeling, or vesicle production, than currently appreciated.
claims.source: In addition to expressing cell adhesion molecules, basal cells exhibited high level expression of several genes involved in membrane trafficking and lipid metabolism (Cd9, Sdc1, Sdc4, Vmp1, Apoe, Apoc1, Sgms2), suggesting that basal cells may exhibit more dynamic membrane remodeling, or vesicle production, than currently appreciated.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data and represents a hypothesis based on gene expression patterns.

claims.claim: It has been suggested that basal cells of the epididymis express antigens common to mononuclear phagocytic cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells and thus may derive from these cells or even overlap with them functionally.
claims.source: It has been suggested that basal cells of the epididymis express antigens common to mononuclear phagocytic cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells and thus may derive from these cells or even overlap with them functionally (Seiler et al., 1999; Seiler et al., 1998; Yeung et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Reclustering of basal and immune cells shows a clear separation between basal cells and immune cells based on gene expression patterns.
claims.source: To explore the relationship between these cell types in our dataset, we extracted all putative basal and immune cells for reclustering. We observe a clear separation between basal cells and immune cells based on gene expression patterns (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B and see below).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B.

claims.claim: Co-staining studies with basal cell markers and mononuclear phagocyte markers were consistent with prior reports showing that basal cells are separate from macrophages and other antigen-presenting cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, our followup co-staining studies with basal cell markers and mononuclear phagocyte markers were consistent with prior reports (Shum et al., 2014) showing that basal cells are separate from macrophages and other antigen-presenting cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The scRNA-Seq data and histology studies confirm that differentiated basal cells are distinct from other cells of the monocyte/macrophage lineage.
claims.source: Together, our scRNA-Seq data and histology studies confirm that differentiated basal cells are distinct from other cells of the monocyte/macrophage lineage.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis and immunofluorescence data.

claims.claim: Reclustering of basal cells revealed little diversity among basal cells.
claims.source: To further explore the diversity of basal cell subtypes in our dataset, we extracted and reclustered the three putative basal cell clusters as described above for principal and clear cells. This analysis revealed little diversity among basal cells (Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 5A–C.

claims.claim: One major subgrouping of basal cell subclusters was based on expression of ribosomal protein genes (RPGs), with the two basal cell subpopulations (RPG high and RPG low) also exhibiting significant differences in the number of UMIs captured per cell.
claims.source: Although we did observe one major subgrouping of basal cell subclusters based on expression of ribosomal protein genes (RPGs), the two basal cell subpopulations (RPG high and RPG low) also exhibited significant differences in the number of UMIs captured per cell (Figure 5C–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 5C–E.

claims.claim: It is unclear whether the RPG-low basal cells represent a biologically meaningful population marked by low biosynthetic activity, or whether these cells represent technical artifacts.
claims.source: Therefore, it is unclear whether the RPG-low basal cells represent a biologically meaningful population marked by low biosynthetic activity, or whether these cells represent technical artifacts (of, say, inefficient lysis and RNA recovery).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of differences in UMI counts between basal cell subpopulations.

claims.claim: One additional cluster of basal cells was identified with a subset expressing high levels of Notch2, Spry2, Pecam1, Slc39a1, Ccl7, Cd93, and Penk.
claims.source: Beyond this major grouping of basal cells, we did identify one additional cluster of possible interest, with a subset of basal cells expressing high levels of Notch2, Spry2, Pecam1, Slc39a1, Ccl7, Cd93, and Penk, although our followup staining efforts to identify this putative basal cell subset were inconclusive (not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subclustering analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Two clusters of muscle cells were identified, defined by their expression of various actomyosin cytoskeletal genes, and are primarily populated by cells from the vas deferens.
claims.source: Two clusters of muscle cells, defined by their expression of various actomyosin cytoskeletal genes (Myh11, Mylk, Acta1, Tpm2, etc.) are identified, and are primarily populated by cells from the vas deferens (Figures 1C and 2) where contraction of the muscular sheath drives sperm movement during ejaculation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figures 1C and 2.

claims.claim: Contraction of the muscular sheath in the vas deferens drives sperm movement during ejaculation.
claims.source: Two clusters of muscle cells, defined by their expression of various actomyosin cytoskeletal genes (Myh11, Mylk, Acta1, Tpm2, etc.) are identified, and are primarily populated by cells from the vas deferens (Figures 1C and 2) where contraction of the muscular sheath drives sperm movement during ejaculation.

results.result: The study generated a comprehensive single-cell atlas of the murine epididymis and vas deferens using 10X Chromium single-cell RNA-Seq, profiling 8880 cells from four anatomical regions (caput, corpus, cauda, vas deferens) pooled from four mice. Bulk RNA-Seq from at least 10 samples per region confirmed expected region-specific gene expression patterns and recapitulated prior microarray studies at improved genomic resolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C31, C36-C41 collectively describe the experimental design and dataset generation. The methods are clearly described with appropriate sample sizes (4 mice, 8 tissue samples pooled per region), technical replicates for bulk RNA-Seq (n≥10), and quality metrics (8880 cells, median 1965 UMIs/cell). The bulk RNA-Seq validation against prior microarray data (Johnston et al., 2005) provides orthogonal confirmation of the approach.

results.result: The single-cell atlas identified all major epididymal cell types including principal cells, clear cells, basal cells, and support cells (fibroblasts, smooth muscle, macrophages, immune cells). Cells are distinguished by two molecular features: cell-type-specific marker genes (e.g., V-ATPase genes in clear cells) and region-specific gene expression in principal cells, suggesting specialized microenvironments along the epididymis.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C45-C50 describe cell type identification using established marker genes and differential expression analysis. The identification of known cell types validates the technical quality of the dataset. The two-feature distinction (cell type vs. regional specialization) is well-supported by the clustering analysis and marker gene expression patterns shown in Figures 2-3.

results.result: Principal cells exhibit extensive regional specialization across the epididymis, with roughly eight distinct gene expression signatures corresponding to anatomical segments. Subclustering identified 3-4 subtypes within each anatomical region (caput, corpus, cauda, vas deferens), concordant with prior microarray studies and supporting the notion that anatomical segmentation generates multiple distinct microenvironments for sperm maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C32-C33, C53-C60, C128-C129 describe regional specialization of principal cells. The subclustering analysis (Figure 3) shows clear separation by anatomical origin, with further subdivision within regions. Comparison to Johnston et al. 2005 microarray data validates the segment assignments. The inference about distinct microenvironments (C50, C60) is reasonable given the extensive regional gene expression differences.

results.result: Region-specific genes in principal cells are predominantly members of multi-gene families organized in genomic clusters, including β-defensins, aldo-keto reductases, lipocalins, serine protease inhibitors, cysteine-rich peptides, and RNaseA family members.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62, C133 describe the genomic organization of region-specific genes. This is supported by the single-cell RNA-seq data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and extensive citations to prior studies documenting these gene families. The observation is consistent with established knowledge of epididymal gene regulation.

results.result: The study identified two distinct populations of clear cells, with one subpopulation (Cluster 2) confined to caput and corpus epididymis expressing Iapp (encoding Amylin). Immunofluorescence confirmed Amylin-positive and Amylin-negative clear cells cohabiting within the same region. These Amylin-positive cells are unlikely to correspond to previously described 'narrow' or 'apical' cells as they are found outside the initial segment and lack Carbonic Anhydrase II enrichment.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C34, C82-C88, C156-C157, C159-C161 describe the discovery of Amylin-positive clear cells. The subclustering analysis (Figure 4B-D) shows clear separation based on Iapp expression, and immunofluorescence validation (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) confirms the presence of both Amylin-positive and Amylin-negative clear cells. The distinction from narrow/apical cells is supported by anatomical distribution data and lack of Car2 enrichment.

results.result: Clear cells are responsible for luminal acidification via high-level expression of V-ATPase genes (Atp6v0c, Atpv1e1, Atp6v1a) and are enriched for genes involved in energy metabolism (to provide ATP for acidification) and membrane trafficking (consistent with V-ATPase localization to microvilli).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C81 describe clear cell function and gene expression. The identification of clear cells by V-ATPase marker genes is well-established and confirmed by the scRNA-seq data (Figure 2B-C). The enrichment for energy metabolism and membrane trafficking genes is supported by the data and represents logical inferences about the cellular requirements for luminal acidification.

results.result: Basal cells were identified by expression of Itga6 and Krt14, with co-expression of cell adhesion and intercellular signaling genes. Subclustering revealed limited diversity, with one major division based on ribosomal protein gene expression that correlated with UMI counts. Basal cells are distinct from immune cells based on gene expression patterns and immunofluorescence co-staining.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94, C97-C101 describe basal cell characterization. The identification by established markers and the distinction from immune cells are well-supported by subclustering analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and immunofluorescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D). The RPG high/low division correlating with UMI counts suggests potential technical artifacts, which the authors appropriately acknowledge.

results.result: The biological significance of RPG-low basal cells and a minor basal cell cluster expressing Notch2, Spry2, Pecam1, Slc39a1, Ccl7, Cd93, and Penk remains uncertain, as these may represent technical artifacts or novel subpopulations requiring further validation.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103 acknowledge uncertainty about specific basal cell subpopulations. The authors appropriately note that RPG-low cells may be technical artifacts due to correlation with UMI counts, and that followup staining for the Notch2+ cluster was inconclusive. This represents honest reporting of uncertain findings that require additional validation.

results.result: Vas deferens principal cells differ from epididymal principal cells in gene expression patterns, with enrichment for transmembrane transporters, signaling molecules, and mitochondrial genes rather than large multi-gene families. Notably, Abcg2 (a xenobiotic transporter) is highly expressed and localized to the apical surface, suggesting a role in concentrating factors in the vas deferens lumen.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C75 describe vas deferens-specific gene expression. The scRNA-seq data clearly shows distinct gene expression patterns in vas deferens principal cells. The Abcg2 localization is confirmed by immunofluorescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), and the inference about luminal concentration (C74-C75) is reasonable based on known ABC transporter function and apical localization, though the specific substrates remain unknown.

results.result: Support cells include muscle cells (primarily from vas deferens), fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and immune cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, lymphocytes). Subclustering revealed limited variation in muscle cells (distinguished by ribosomal protein gene expression) and immune cell populations concordant with prior histological studies, though insufficient cell numbers prevented identification of B cells or T cell subpopulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C111 describe support cell populations. The identification of these cell types by established markers is well-supported by the clustering analysis (Figures 2, 6). The concordance with prior studies validates the findings. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations in resolving rare cell types (B cells) and subpopulations (T cell subtypes) due to insufficient cell numbers.

results.result: Stromal cell subclustering identified functionally specialized subpopulations, including myoid cells (high muscle marker expression) and two vas deferens-specific subtypes: 'stem-like' cells expressing stem cell markers (Angpt1, Lgr5, Tspan8) and 'secretory fibroblasts' expressing numerous intercellular signaling molecules (Il6, Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Cxcl12, Ccl2, Ccl7, Vcam1, Igf1, Ptx3, Tslp). Immunofluorescence confirmed distinct spatial localization of these populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C112-C116 describe stromal cell diversity. The subclustering analysis (Figure 6D-F) shows clear separation of stromal subtypes with distinct marker gene expression. The immunofluorescence validation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) confirms the spatial organization with Lgr5+ cells at the periphery and Ptx3/Tslp+ cells closer to the lumen. The functional annotations are reasonable hypotheses based on marker gene expression.

results.result: Ligand-receptor analysis predicted intercellular signaling networks between cell types, identifying significant interactions (p<0.01) including complementary ligand-receptor expression between basal cells and endothelial cells, and reciprocal connections between macrophages and secretory fibroblasts in the vas deferens (where macrophages were enriched, p<10⁻⁷).
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C117-C123 describe predicted cell-cell communication networks. The ligand-receptor analysis uses an established database (Ramilowski et al., 2015) and appropriate statistical testing (hypergeometric test, p<0.01). The spatial juxtaposition of basal cells and endothelial cells supports the predicted interaction. The macrophage enrichment in vas deferens is statistically significant. However, these remain predictions requiring experimental validation.

results.result: Within principal cell clusters, individual cells show heterogeneous expression of marker genes consistent with prior immunostaining studies of patchy protein expression. These highly variable markers exhibit little co-expression, suggesting stochastic expression of individual genes rather than coordinated programs, though whether this reflects stable subspecialization or transient asynchronous expression requires future live-cell imaging studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C132 describe cell-to-cell heterogeneity within principal cell clusters. The observation is supported by the scRNA-seq data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3) and is consistent with prior immunostaining studies. The inference about stochastic vs. coordinated expression is reasonable based on lack of co-expression. The authors appropriately acknowledge that distinguishing stable vs. transient heterogeneity requires additional experiments.

results.result: The study presents a comprehensive single-cell atlas of the murine epididymis and vas deferens that recovers all previously described cell types, documents complete molecular profiles, identifies markers for potentially novel cell types (Amylin-positive clear cells, vas deferens-specific fibroblast subtypes), and provides a resource for hypothesis generation and future studies of epididymal biology.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127, C164-C168 summarize the overall contribution of the study. The comprehensive nature of the dataset is well-supported by the recovery of known cell types, identification of novel subpopulations with validation, and detailed molecular characterization. The dataset represents a significant advance in understanding epididymal cellular composition and provides a valuable resource for the field.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on established knowledge of epididymal biology, including sperm maturation processes, anatomical organization, regional gene expression, cell types, and functional roles. This contextualizes the single-cell atlas within the broader field of reproductive biology.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C9-C30, C51-C53, C63-C64, C89-C92, C105, C148, C153-C154 represent established knowledge in reproductive biology, supported by extensive citations throughout the manuscript. These claims provide essential context for interpreting the single-cell data and are appropriately referenced to prior literature.

results.result: The Discussion contextualizes region-specific gene families within known epididymal functions including sperm membrane/glycocalyx remodeling, antimicrobial defense, redox regulation, biosynthesis of signaling molecules (prostaglandins), small molecule binding (lipocalins), protease regulation (serine protease inhibitors), and RNA processing (RNases producing tRNA fragments).
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C147 synthesize the functional implications of region-specific gene expression patterns. These interpretations are well-supported by extensive citations to prior research and represent reasonable connections between the observed gene expression patterns and known epididymal functions. Some claims (C136, C141-C142, C144-C147) include speculative elements appropriately qualified by the authors.

results.result: The Discussion draws parallels between epididymal gene expression gradients and kidney nephrons/collecting ducts, noting shared expression of genes (Aqp, Fxyd, Cry, Akr, Tspan families) and similar cell types (V-ATPase+ cells, Krt5+ basal-like cells), while identifying epididymis-specific genes (Rnase9-12, Cst family) that may be specific to sperm maturation functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C152 compare epididymis to kidney biology. The comparison is supported by citations to kidney single-cell studies (Ransick et al., 2019) and represents a reasonable inference based on shared tubular architecture and pH regulation functions. The identification of epididymis-specific genes provides a useful framework for distinguishing general tubular epithelial functions from sperm maturation-specific processes.

results.result: The Discussion notes that Amylin-positive clear cells are enriched in the caput epididymis where morphologically distinctive 'narrow' and 'apical' clear cells have been described, and suggests future studies should investigate functional differences between Amylin-positive and -negative clear cells, particularly given Amylin's role in systemic metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C158, C162-C163 provide context for the Amylin-positive clear cell discovery and suggest future directions. The historical context is appropriately cited, and the suggestion for future functional studies is reasonable given the novelty of the finding. The speculation about local vs. systemic Amylin signaling is appropriately qualified.

results.result: The study used 10-12 week old male FVB/NJ mice with all procedures approved by the University of Massachusetts Medical School IACUC (Protocol # A-1833-18).
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C170 describe the experimental animals and ethical compliance. These are straightforward methodological details that are appropriately documented.
